Data Representation

Compression Lab

Year 10, 1.2 L5 · Compression · 30 minutes

  • Concept: Why files get compressed, and the two ways it can be done.
  • Challenge: Encode and decode your own pixel row using run-length encoding.
  • Exam link: Two real Cambridge questions on choosing and explaining a compression method.
  • Plenary: Back to file size calculations, from memory.

steps.label: Why Compress a File?
steps.content:
Why Compress a File?

Every file size calculation this topic has produced a number - and that number is often inconveniently large. Compression makes a file smaller so it takes up less storage and travels faster over a network, without changing what the file actually contains. There are two completely different ways to achieve that:

  • Lossless compression - the file can be decompressed back to an exact copy of the original, bit for bit. Nothing is thrown away, only stored more efficiently.
  • Lossy compression - some of the original data is permanently removed, chosen because it is judged least noticeable. This gives a much smaller file, but the original can never be perfectly restored.

Neither is simply better - the right choice depends on whether losing a little quality is acceptable for what the file will be used for.

steps.label: Challenge: Run-Length Encoding
steps.content:
Challenge: Run-Length Encoding

Run-length encoding (RLE) is a lossless method: instead of storing every pixel individually, it stores each unbroken run as (how many, which colour). Paint the row, then read the encoded string underneath it - or type your own encoding and press Decode to paint the row from it.

Try the two presets. Notice RLE only helps when there are long runs of the same colour - a row that alternates every pixel can end up needing MORE numbers stored than the original, not fewer.

steps.label: Exam Question: Choosing Lossless
steps.content:
Exam Question: Choosing Lossless

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, February/March 2025, Question 2. An artist compresses an image file before uploading it to their website, so users can download it to print as a poster. The artist compresses it using lossless compression.

items.prompt: (b) Describe the relationship between the resolution of an image and its file size.
items.modelAnswer: As resolution increases (more pixels), file size increases, because there are more pixels to store data for. Doubling the resolution in both directions roughly quadruples the file size, since the total number of pixels is width multiplied by height.

items.prompt: (c)(i) Explain the reasons why the artist chose lossless compression instead of lossy compression for this image file.
items.modelAnswer: Lossless compression does not remove any of the original data, so no quality is lost when the file is compressed and decompressed. This matters here because the image will be printed as a large poster, where any loss of detail from lossy compression would be clearly visible. Lossy compression would give a smaller file, but the drop in quality would not be an acceptable trade-off for a printed poster.

items.prompt: (c)(ii) Identify one lossless method of compressing an image, and describe your chosen method.
items.modelAnswer: Method: run-length encoding (RLE). Description: RLE looks for runs of repeated, identical values (for example, the same pixel colour repeated many times in a row) and stores each run as a single (count, value) pair instead of storing every repeated value individually. This reduces file size when there are long runs of the same value, without losing any of the original data - decompressing exactly rebuilds the original pixels.

steps.label: Exam Question: Choosing Lossy
steps.content:
Exam Question: Choosing Lossy

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, June 2021, Question 2. Jolene displays videos on her website. She uses lossy compression to reduce the file size of the videos.

items.prompt: (a) Describe how lossy compression reduces the file size of the videos.
items.modelAnswer: Lossy compression permanently removes some of the data from the file - data judged least important or least noticeable to a viewer, such as very small differences in colour or fine detail the human eye is unlikely to notice. Because less data has to be stored, the file becomes smaller. This removed data cannot be recovered afterwards, so the video can never be restored to its exact original quality.

steps.label: Exam Question: Why Lossy for Video
steps.content:
Exam Question: Why Lossy for Video

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, June 2021, Question 2 asked for two reasons Jolene would choose lossy over lossless compression for the videos on her website.

items.prompt: Reason 1: why is lossy compression a good choice for videos on a website?
options: It makes the file much smaller, so it downloads or streams faster and uses less storage
It lets the video be reconstructed exactly, with no data lost
It plays the video back at a higher frame rate
It removes the need to store the audio track
items.explain: A much smaller file is quicker to send over a network and cheaper to store - the main reason lossy is used for streamed video.

items.prompt: Reason 2: why is losing some of the data acceptable here?
options: The small drop in quality is hard for a viewer to notice while the video plays
Video files never contain any important data
The lost data is automatically restored when the video is downloaded
Lossless compression cannot be used on video at all
items.explain: Lossy compression removes detail a viewer is unlikely to notice, so the quality loss is an acceptable trade for the smaller file.

steps.label: Checked Practice
steps.content:
Checked Practice

Total: 2 marks

items.prompt: Which kind of image would run-length encoding compress well?
options: A flag or simple logo with large blocks of one solid colour
A detailed photograph of a forest
A picture where every pixel is a slightly different colour
items.explain: RLE only shrinks data when there are long runs of identical pixels. Big flat areas of one colour compress well; noisy detail does not.

steps.content:
Plenary

Answer from memory - no notes, no going back to the challenges. Both questions are real Cambridge exam questions.

Total: 5 marks

y10_1_2_l5_practice.feedback: Count the runs of identical colour - each run is one pair.
Add up every count in the encoding.

y10_1_2_l5_plenary.feedback: Multiply height x width x colour depth (in bits), then divide by 8 for bytes.
With colour depth already given in bytes, multiply the pixel count directly by the colour depth - no need to convert to bits first.
